title: Short Stuff: Death Cap Mushroom
summary: Short Stuff episode on the death cap mushroom (Amanita phalloides). The hosts open with jokes about the name and a band of the same name, then cover its lethality (a cited 10 to 15 percent fatality rate), its life as an ectomycorrhizal fungus partnered with oak and beech trees, and how it likely reached North America via imported European trees, with the first known sightings in 1938 at the Del Monte Hotel in California. They discuss invasiveness in California woodlands versus urban East Coast settings, the 2016 San Francisco Bay Area outbreak that sickened fourteen people, and the toxins alpha-amanitin and phallotoxins, which damage the liver and kidneys with delayed symptoms. They note liver transplants may be needed, discuss organ waiting lists, and close with foraging safety advice and identification tips such as olive-green coloring and brown striations on the cap.

segments.title: Opening banter and band name joke
segments.summary: The hosts open the short episode and joke about the name Death Cap sounding like a metal band, comparing it to Death Cab for Cutie and the Postal Service.

segments.title: Fatality rate and eating mushrooms
segments.summary: The hosts say eating death cap can be fatal, with a cited fatality rate of 10 to 15 percent, compare it to white button mushrooms, and banter about mushroom texture.

segments.title: 2016 Bay Area outbreak and mycorrhizal relationship
segments.summary: Speaker describes a 2016 outbreak in the San Francisco Bay Area where fourteen people were sickened, one child with permanent neurological damage. Josh explains the fungus forms a mutualistic relationship with oak and beech tree roots, trading nitrogen for sugars.

segments.title: How the death cap arrived in North America
segments.summary: The hosts discuss that the fungus likely came over on an imported European tree. The first known North American sightings were in 1938 at the Del Monte Hotel in California, and it has since spread to the East Coast and other parts of the world. They mention Cheech Marin and a joke about him eating one.

segments.title: Sponsor break
segments.summary: Break in the episode before the return to the discussion.

segments.title: Invasiveness and the scientific source
segments.summary: The hosts discuss what invasive means for the death cap, which is invasive in California woodlands but less so in East Coast urban parks. They credit the How Stuff Works article and an interview with Professor Pringle at the University of Wisconsin-Madison.

segments.title: Toxins, symptoms, and liver transplants
segments.summary: Phallotoxins cause dehydration, vomiting, and kidney damage, while amatoxin shuts down RNA transcription and cell function and destroys the liver. Symptoms fade early, giving a false sense of safety. Patients may need liver transplants, and the hosts discuss transplant waiting lists.

segments.title: Foraging safety and identification
segments.summary: The hosts advise against eating death caps and urge caution for foragers, recommending knowledgeable guides. Identification features mentioned are olive-green tinge and brown striations on the cap, plus fairy rings around the stem. They note the mushroom tastes good, which is why people eat it.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: The hosts close the short episode with a joke and the standard iHeartRadio production credit.
